q: Plant cells usually have a fixed, regular shape, while animal cells are often irregular or rounded. This difference is mainly due to the:
o: Rigid cell wall of plant cells
Presence of centrioles in plant cells
Absence of a plasma membrane in animal cells
x: The rigid cellulose wall holds a plant cell in a fixed shape. Animal cells have only a flexible plasma membrane, so their shape can vary.

q: Most eukaryotic cells have a diameter in the range of about:
x: Eukaryotic cells are typically 10–100 µm across, roughly ten times larger than most prokaryotic cells (about 1–10 µm).

q: The nucleus was discovered in plant cells in 1831 by:
x: Robert Brown described the nucleus in orchid cells in 1831. Robert Hooke named the cell in 1665, and Golgi described the Golgi apparatus.

q: The term 'chromosome' was first used in 1888 by:
x: Waldeyer coined the word chromosome in 1888 for the threads that take up stain in a dividing nucleus. Mendel worked on inheritance, and Watson on DNA structure.

q: In a mature plant cell, the nucleus usually lies near the cell wall rather than in the centre because:
o: The cell wall attracts the nucleus
The large central vacuole pushes the cytoplasm and nucleus to the edge
Plant cells have no cytoplasm in the centre of young cells
Centrioles pull the nucleus to one side
x: The big central vacuole takes up most of the volume of a mature plant cell, pressing the cytoplasm and nucleus against the wall. In animal cells the nucleus is usually central.

q: Prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria and cyanobacteria are placed in the kingdom:
x: All prokaryotes are grouped in kingdom Monera, also called Prokaryotae. Protists, fungi and plants are all eukaryotic.

q: Mature red blood cells of mammals have no nucleus. As a result, they:
o: Carry less haemoglobin than other cells
Can divide faster than other cells
Are able to carry out aerobic respiration better
Cannot divide or make new proteins
x: Without a nucleus a cell has no genes to direct protein synthesis or cell division, so mature red cells cannot divide and live only about 120 days. Losing the nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin.

q: Chromosomes become clearly visible under a light microscope:
o: During cell division, when the chromatin condenses
x: In interphase the chromatin is long and thin; during cell division it coils up into thick, short chromosomes that can be seen and counted.

q: Compared with a typical plant cell, a typical animal cell has vacuoles that are:
o: Bounded by a tonoplast filled with cell sap
x: Animal cells have small, often temporary vacuoles, such as food and water vacuoles. A single large central vacuole with cell sap is typical of mature plant cells.

q: Which statement correctly compares the DNA of a eukaryotic nucleus with that of a bacterium?
o: Eukaryotic DNA is a single circular molecule without proteins
Bacterial DNA is enclosed in a nuclear envelope
Eukaryotic DNA is linear, divided into several chromosomes and bound to histones
Bacterial DNA is divided into many linear chromosomes
x: Eukaryotic nuclei hold several linear chromosomes in which DNA is packed with histones. A bacterium has one circular DNA molecule lying free in the nucleoid.

q: Each skeletal muscle fibre contains many nuclei. Such a cell is described as:
x: A skeletal muscle fibre forms by fusion of many cells, so it has many nuclei and is multinucleate. Enucleate means having no nucleus, as in mature red blood cells.

q: In a nucleus at interphase, the genetic material appears as a network of fine threads called:
x: Between divisions DNA and its proteins are spread out as a fine chromatin network. Chromatids are the condensed halves of a replicated chromosome seen during division.

q: Lysosomes are common in animal cells. In most plant cells, much of the role of lysosomes is taken over by the:
x: Lysosomes are rare in plant cells; their large vacuole contains hydrolytic enzymes and breaks down unwanted materials.

q: In many bacteria, infoldings of the plasma membrane that are thought to help in respiration and DNA replication are called:
x: Mesosomes are inward folds of the bacterial plasma membrane. Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which bacteria do not have.

q: The narrow space between the inner and outer membranes of the nuclear envelope is called the:
x: The two nuclear membranes are separated by the perinuclear space, which is continuous with the lumen of the ER. Nucleoplasm is the fluid inside the inner membrane.

q: The diploid number of chromosomes in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is:
x: Drosophila has 8 chromosomes (4 pairs) in its body cells, which makes it a useful organism for genetics. Humans have 46.

q: During cytokinesis, a plant cell divides by forming a:
o: Cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two
Cell plate across the middle of the cell
Pair of new centrioles at the equator
x: A rigid wall cannot be pinched in, so plant cells build a cell plate from Golgi vesicles that grows outwards into a new wall. Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow.

q: In prokaryotic cells, translation of an mRNA can begin while the mRNA is still being transcribed. This is possible because:
o: Prokaryotic mRNA is made in the nucleolus
There is no nuclear envelope separating DNA from ribosomes
x: With no nuclear envelope, ribosomes can attach to an mRNA as soon as it starts to come off the DNA. In eukaryotes, mRNA must first leave the nucleus through nuclear pores.

q: During cell division, the nucleolus:
o: Disappears in prophase and reappears in telophase
x: The nucleolus breaks down in early prophase and is formed again at the nucleolar organiser regions in telophase, when the nuclei re-form.

q: A small knob at the end of a chromosome, separated from the rest of the arm by a secondary constriction, is called a:
x: Chromosomes with a satellite are called SAT chromosomes; the satellite is joined to the arm across a secondary constriction. The centromere is the primary constriction.

q: A palisade cell of a leaf contains an organelle that a liver cell does not. This organelle is the:
x: Chloroplasts are found only in photosynthetic cells such as leaf palisade cells. Mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and ribosomes occur in both.

q: In the Gram stain, Gram-positive bacteria appear:
o: Pink, because they lose the crystal violet stain
Colourless, because they take up no stain
Purple, because their thick peptidoglycan wall keeps the crystal violet stain
x: Thick peptidoglycan in Gram-positive walls holds the crystal violet–iodine complex, so they stay purple. Gram-negative bacteria lose it and take up the pink counterstain.

q: The endoplasmic reticulum was first described from electron micrographs in 1945 by:
x: K. R. Porter, with Claude and Fullam, first described the ER in 1945 using the electron microscope. Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model.

q: The main function of chromosomes is to:
o: Carry genes and pass hereditary information to daughter cells
x: Chromosomes carry the genes made of DNA and hand an exact copy of them to each daughter cell at division.

q: In the cells of higher plants, the mitotic spindle forms without centrioles. Such a spindle, having no asters at its poles, is called:
x: Asters form around centrioles, which higher plant cells lack, so their spindle is anastral. Animal cells, with centrioles, form an astral spindle.

q: Bacteria do not reproduce sexually, but some can transfer DNA from one cell to another through a sex pilus. This process is called:
x: In conjugation, DNA (often a plasmid) passes from a donor to a recipient bacterium through a sex pilus. Binary fission is asexual division, and meiosis does not occur in prokaryotes.

q: The endoplasmic reticulum exists in three forms, which are:
x: ER is a network of flattened sacs (cisternae), branching tubules and small vesicles. Grana and stroma belong to chloroplasts; cristae and matrix to mitochondria.

q: A gene is best described as:
o: A segment of DNA that codes for a particular protein or trait
x: A gene is a stretch of DNA at a definite place on a chromosome; each chromosome carries many genes.

q: Besides cellulose, the primary cell wall of a plant cell contains:
x: The primary wall has cellulose microfibrils set in a matrix of hemicellulose and pectin. Chitin is found in fungal walls and peptidoglycan in bacterial walls.

q: Ribosomes in a eukaryotic cell occur both free in the cytoplasm and attached to the ER, but in a prokaryotic cell they:
o: Are attached only to the nuclear envelope
Lie only free in the cytoplasm, because there is no ER
Are attached only to the cell wall
x: Prokaryotes have no endoplasmic reticulum, so all their ribosomes are free in the cytoplasm.

q: Which pairing of an ER type with a main product is correct?
o: Smooth ER – lipids such as phospholipids and steroids
x: Smooth ER makes lipids, including membrane phospholipids and steroids. Rough ER, with its ribosomes, makes proteins such as secretory enzymes.

q: The fixed position that a gene occupies on a chromosome is called its:
x: A gene's locus is its specific place on a chromosome. Alleles are alternative forms of a gene found at the same locus.

q: Small areas of a plant cell wall where secondary wall material is not laid down, so that the wall stays thin, are called:
x: Pits are thin regions in the secondary wall, usually opposite pits of neighbouring cells, which help water and solutes pass. Plasmodesmata are cytoplasmic strands passing through the wall.

q: Cyanobacteria resemble green plants because they:
o: Have chloroplasts surrounded by double membranes
Have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope
Have cell walls made of cellulose
Contain chlorophyll a and give off oxygen in photosynthesis
x: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes without chloroplasts, but they have chlorophyll a on internal membranes and release oxygen as plants do. Their walls contain peptidoglycan.

q: Proteins made on the ribosomes of the rough ER first pass into the:
o: Lumen of the ER cisternae, where they are folded and transported
x: Proteins made on RER enter the ER lumen, where they fold and may be modified before travelling in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus.

q: Alleles of a gene are found:
o: At different loci on the same chromosome
At the same locus on a pair of homologous chromosomes
x: Alleles are alternative forms of one gene, such as tall and dwarf, and they sit at matching loci on the two homologous chromosomes.

q: The walls of cork cells become impermeable to water and gases because of the deposition of:
x: Suberin, a waxy substance laid in the walls of cork cells, makes them waterproof. Pectin, cellulose and hemicellulose are normal wall components that let water pass.

q: Which of the following eukaryotic cells has no cell wall?
x: Plants and most algae have cellulose walls and fungi have chitin walls, but animal cells are bounded only by the plasma membrane.

q: The Golgi apparatus is made of a stack of:
x: Each Golgi body (dictyosome) is a stack of flattened cisternae with vesicles at their edges. Cristae belong to mitochondria and thylakoids to chloroplasts.

q: Besides DNA and histones, chromosomes also contain small amounts of:
x: Chromosomes are mostly DNA and histones, with small amounts of RNA and non-histone proteins such as enzymes and regulatory proteins.

q: The thickness of the plasma membrane is about:
x: The plasma membrane is roughly 7–10 nm thick, so it can only be resolved with an electron microscope.

q: According to the endosymbiont hypothesis, chloroplasts arose from:
o: Photosynthetic prokaryotes, like cyanobacteria, taken into an early eukaryotic cell
Vesicles budded off the Golgi apparatus
x: Chloroplasts are thought to descend from cyanobacteria-like cells engulfed by an ancestral eukaryote; their own DNA, 70S ribosomes and double membranes support this.

q: Secretory vesicles bud off from the Golgi apparatus at its:
x: Vesicles from the ER join the cis face; the finished products leave in vesicles from the trans face, which faces the plasma membrane.

q: The core of a nucleosome contains two molecules each of the histones:
x: The histone octamer is two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. H1 is not part of the core; it binds the linker DNA outside it.

q: Proteins loosely attached to the inner or outer surface of the plasma membrane, without passing through the lipid bilayer, are called:
x: Peripheral proteins sit on the surface and are easily removed. Integral proteins, including channel proteins, are embedded in or span the bilayer.

q: Mitochondria are thought to have come from bacteria. One piece of evidence is that new mitochondria:
o: Are made fresh by the Golgi apparatus
Arise by division of existing mitochondria, much like binary fission
Are assembled from parts of the nuclear envelope
Arise from vacuoles in the cytoplasm
x: Mitochondria are never made from scratch; they grow and divide like bacteria. Together with their circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, this supports their bacterial origin.

q: The Golgi apparatus of plant cells synthesises wall polysaccharides that are not made at the plasma membrane. These are:
x: Cellulose is made at the plasma membrane, but pectins and hemicelluloses are made in the Golgi and carried to the wall in vesicles.

q: A person with the karyotype 47,XXY develops as a male. This shows that, in humans, maleness is mainly determined by:
o: The presence of a Y chromosome
x: Despite having two X chromosomes, an XXY person (Klinefelter syndrome) is male, because a gene on the Y chromosome triggers male development.

q: Cells lining the small intestine have many tiny finger-like extensions of the plasma membrane called microvilli. Their main role is to:
o: Increase the surface area for absorption
Move food along the gut by beating
x: Microvilli greatly increase the absorbing surface. They do not beat; movement of material by beating is done by cilia.

q: Bacteria can be classified by shape. A rod-shaped bacterium is called a:
x: Rod-shaped bacteria are bacilli, spherical ones are cocci, spiral ones are spirilla, and comma-shaped ones are vibrios.

q: The acrosome at the tip of a sperm head, which contains enzymes to penetrate the egg, is formed from the:
x: The acrosome is a large vesicle produced by the Golgi apparatus, filled with enzymes that digest a path through the layers around the egg.

q: A girl's karyotype shows 45 chromosomes with only one X chromosome and no Y. She has:
x: Turner syndrome is 45,X: a female with a single X chromosome. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY, and Down syndrome is trisomy 21.

q: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated salt solution. It loses water and its cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall. This is called:
x: Water leaves the vacuole by osmosis, so the protoplast pulls away from the rigid wall: plasmolysis. Haemolysis is the bursting of red cells, and crenation is the shrinking of an animal cell, which has no wall.

q: Antibiotics such as streptomycin and tetracycline stop protein synthesis in bacteria but do much less harm to human cells. This is because they act on:
o: Peptidoglycan, which is absent from human cells
Mitochondria, which bacteria have in large numbers
70S ribosomes, which differ from the 80S ribosomes in human cytoplasm
x: These drugs bind to bacterial 70S ribosomes. Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so most human protein synthesis is unaffected. Penicillin, not these drugs, acts on peptidoglycan.

q: The outer and inner membranes of a mitochondrion differ in that:
o: The outer membrane is folded into cristae
The inner membrane carries ribosomes on its outer surface
Only the outer membrane contains proteins
The outer membrane is smooth and more permeable, while the inner one is folded and less permeable
x: The outer membrane is smooth and has pores that let small molecules through; the inner membrane is folded into cristae and controls movement of materials tightly.

q: Chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes are called:
x: Autosomes are all chromosomes except the sex chromosomes (X and Y); humans have 44 autosomes. Sex chromosomes are also called allosomes.

q: Cilia and flagella of eukaryotic cells show a pattern of microtubules in cross-section described as:
x: The shaft of a cilium or flagellum has nine outer doublets around two central microtubules (9 + 2). The 9 triplet pattern is seen in centrioles and basal bodies.

q: Some bacteria, such as Bacillus and Clostridium, survive boiling and drying by forming:
x: Endospores are tough, dormant structures formed inside the cell, which resist heat, drying and chemicals. A capsule protects against phagocytosis but not against boiling.

q: Stalked particles on the inner surface of the cristae, called F1 particles or oxysomes, are the sites of:
x: The F1 particles are ATP synthase enzymes that make ATP using energy from electron transport. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

q: Immediately after the centromeres split at anaphase of mitosis, a human cell contains a total of:
x: Each of the 46 chromosomes separates into two chromatids, and each chromatid now counts as a chromosome, so there are 92 until the cell divides.

q: The basal body found at the base of each cilium or flagellum is similar in structure to a:
x: A basal body, like a centriole, is a cylinder of nine microtubule triplets; in fact basal bodies arise from centrioles.

q: A typical bacterium has one circular chromosome, so with respect to its main genes it is:
x: With only one copy of each main gene on its single chromosome, a bacterium is haploid. Most body cells of plants and animals are diploid.

q: The DNA and ribosomes of a mitochondrion are found in its:
x: The matrix contains circular mitochondrial DNA, 70S ribosomes and the enzymes of the Krebs cycle.

q: Very large chromosomes, made of many DNA strands lying side by side, are found in the salivary glands of Drosophila larvae. They are called:
x: Polytene chromosomes form when DNA replicates many times without the cell dividing, so the copies stay together. Lampbrush chromosomes are found in developing egg cells.

q: In a chloroplast, chlorophyll is located in the:
x: Chlorophyll and other pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes, which are stacked into grana. The stroma is the fluid around them.

q: The term 'eukaryotic' comes from Greek roots describing a cell with a:
x: Eu means true and karyon means nucleus, so eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus surrounded by a nuclear envelope.

q: Flight muscle cells of insects need much ATP. Compared with less active cells, their mitochondria would be expected to have:
x: More cristae mean more inner membrane area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so active cells have mitochondria with many cristae.

q: Chemically, the DNA of a chromosome is a polymer of:
x: DNA is a long chain of deoxyribonucleotides, each made of deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogenous base. Ribonucleotides make up RNA.

q: The Calvin cycle (the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis) takes place in the:
x: The enzymes that fix carbon dioxide are dissolved in the stroma. The light-dependent reactions occur on the thylakoid membranes.

q: Which type of genetic element is widely used as a vector to carry foreign genes into bacteria in genetic engineering?
x: Plasmids are small circular DNA molecules that replicate on their own; a gene inserted into a plasmid can be copied in the bacterium.

q: Which stage of aerobic respiration does NOT take place inside the mitochondrion?
o: Oxidation of pyruvate to acetyl CoA
x: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondrion, where its oxidation, the Krebs cycle and electron transport take place.

q: Telomeres become slightly shorter each time a normal body cell divides. This is linked with:
o: Ageing and the limited number of divisions of a cell
x: Each round of DNA replication leaves the chromosome ends a little shorter; when telomeres become too short the cell stops dividing, which is linked with ageing.

q: The red, purple and blue colours of many petals are due to water-soluble anthocyanin pigments stored in the:
x: Anthocyanins are dissolved in the cell sap of the vacuole. Chromoplasts hold fat-soluble carotenoids, which give yellow and orange colours.

q: Eukaryotic plasma membranes usually contain sterols such as cholesterol. Most bacterial membranes:
o: Contain more cholesterol than animal cells
x: Sterols are a typical part of eukaryotic membranes; most bacteria lack them (mycoplasmas are an exception, taking sterols from their hosts).

q: Pancreatic cells are given radioactive amino acids for a few minutes. Shortly afterwards, most of the radioactivity is found first in the:
x: Labelled amino acids are built into proteins on the ribosomes of the rough ER, so the label appears there first and only later in the Golgi and secretory vesicles.

q: During cell division, chromatin coils up tightly into short, thick chromosomes. The main advantage of this is that:
o: Genes can be transcribed more quickly
Chromosomes can be separated without tangling or breaking
x: Long thin chromatin would tangle and break when pulled apart; compact chromosomes are moved easily by the spindle. Condensed chromatin is actually less active in transcription.

q: When a green tomato ripens and turns red, its plastids change from:
x: During ripening chlorophyll breaks down and the chloroplasts become chromoplasts rich in red carotenoids such as lycopene.

q: Compared with a large eukaryotic cell, a small bacterial cell has a:
o: Smaller surface area to volume ratio, so it exchanges materials slowly
Smaller ratio, so it needs no plasma membrane
Larger surface area to volume ratio, so materials are exchanged rapidly
Larger ratio, so it needs a nuclear envelope
x: Small cells have more surface for each unit of volume, so diffusion can supply all of the cell quickly. Large eukaryotic cells rely on internal membranes and transport.

q: Which pair of organelles is bounded by a double membrane?
x: The nucleus has a double nuclear envelope and the mitochondrion has outer and inner membranes. Golgi, lysosome, ER and vacuole have single membranes; ribosomes and centrioles have none.

q: Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is called:
x: Linked genes travel together because they are on one chromosome. Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.

q: Specialised plastids that store oils are elaioplasts, while those that store proteins are:
x: Aleuroplasts store protein and elaioplasts store oils; amyloplasts store starch. All three are types of colourless leucoplast.

q: Under the electron microscope, a cell shows a nucleus with a double envelope, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes and a cell wall made of chitin. The cell belongs to a:
x: A nucleus, mitochondria and 80S ribosomes mark a eukaryote; a chitin wall shows it is a fungus. Plants have cellulose walls and animals have no wall.

q: The mitochondria of a sperm cell are packed in its:
x: The middle piece is packed with mitochondria that supply ATP for the beating of the tail.

q: Down syndrome usually arises because the parent's gamete carried an extra chromosome 21. This extra chromosome is most often due to:
x: Nondisjunction is the failure of homologous chromosomes or chromatids to separate in meiosis, so a gamete receives two copies of chromosome 21 instead of one.

q: Microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, which help in cell movement and change of shape, are made of the protein:
x: Microfilaments are thin actin fibres. Microtubules, by contrast, are made of tubulin.

q: Which of the following organisms has eukaryotic cells?
x: Yeast is a unicellular fungus with a true nucleus. E. coli and Streptococcus are bacteria and Nostoc is a cyanobacterium, all prokaryotes.

q: In grafting experiments on the single-celled alga Acetabularia, the cap that finally forms, after any first mixed cap is removed, matches the species that supplied the:
x: Hämmerling showed that the cap formed depends on the nucleus, not the stalk, proving that the nucleus holds the information controlling the cell's form.

q: In the cell cycle, chromosomes replicate their DNA during the:
x: DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase, so each chromosome enters mitosis as two sister chromatids.

q: A cell under the microscope has a nucleus, a pair of centrioles, small vacuoles and glycogen granules, but no cell wall. It is most likely:
o: A cell of a flowering plant
x: Centrioles, glycogen and the lack of a wall point to an animal cell. A nucleus rules out bacteria and cyanobacteria.

q: Cytoplasmic streaming and membrane-bound organelles are features of:
x: Eukaryotic cytoplasm streams and contains membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells show no cytoplasmic streaming and have no such organelles.

q: Most of the DNA of a eukaryotic cell is found in the:
x: Nearly all the cell's DNA is in the chromosomes of the nucleus; mitochondria carry only a small circular DNA, and the Golgi and ribosomes have none.
